name: Judaism
date_note: Israelite religion is attested in the Iron Age hill country from about 1200 BCE; worship of one God alone takes its lasting shape around the Babylonian exile (6th c. BCE). Tradition dates Abraham earlier.
summary: The covenant religion of the people of Israel, centred on the Torah. After the Temple's destruction in 70 CE it continued as rabbinic Judaism, the root of every Jewish movement today.

name: Samaritanism
date_note: The Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim was built around the 5th–4th c. BCE; Samaritans see themselves as the direct heirs of ancient Israel rather than a branch of Judaism.
summary: An Israelite religion with its own five-book Torah and its holy mountain at Gerizim. It survives today as a community of under a thousand people.

name: Karaite Judaism
date_note: Traced to Anan ben David in Baghdad around 760; the name Karaite is used from the 9th c.
summary: A Jewish movement that accepts the written Hebrew Bible alone and rejects the authority of the rabbinic oral law.

name: Hasidic Judaism
date_note: Grows around Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov, in the 1740s.
summary: A revival movement of joyful, mystical piety led by rebbes, now central to Orthodox Jewish life in New York and Israel.

name: Orthodox Judaism
date_note: Rabbinic practice is ancient; 'Orthodox' as a self-conscious movement forms in early-19th-c. Central Europe, in answer to Reform.
summary: The movements that hold the written and oral law as binding and unchanged, organised as such in reply to the Jewish Enlightenment and Reform.

name: Reform Judaism
date_note: Israel Jacobson opened his reformed temple at Seesen in 1810.
summary: A movement that treats Jewish law as evolving, with services in the vernacular and full equality of women and men.

name: Conservative Judaism
date_note: The Jewish Theological Seminary was founded in New York in 1886; its ideas go back to Zecharias Frankel in Breslau in the 1840s.
summary: A middle path that keeps Jewish law binding while studying it historically and letting it change.

name: Christianity
date_note: From the ministry and death of Jesus of Nazareth, about 30 CE. There is no year 0.
summary: Faith in Jesus as the Messiah and Son of God. It began as a Jewish movement in Jerusalem and is now the largest religion in the world.

name: Church of the East
date_note: Separates after the Council of Ephesus (431) and declares independence at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 424–486.
summary: The church of the Persian empire, which carried Christianity along the Silk Road to China by 635. Today it continues as the Assyrian Church of the East.

name: Oriental Orthodoxy
date_note: These churches did not accept the Council of Chalcedon in 451.
summary: The Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Armenian, Syriac and Malankara churches, which share a Christology older than Chalcedon.

name: Eastern Orthodoxy
date_note: 1054 is the conventional date of the East–West schism; the break deepened over centuries, especially after 1204.
summary: The churches in communion with Constantinople, including the Greek, Russian, Serbian and Romanian churches.

name: Catholicism
date_note: The Roman church is far older; 1054 marks the conventional East–West schism, after which it is a separate communion.
summary: The church in communion with the Bishop of Rome, the largest single Christian body.

name: Protestantism
date_note: Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses, Wittenberg, 1517.
summary: The churches of the Reformation, which put scripture and faith above church tradition.

name: Lutheranism
date_note: The Augsburg Confession of 1530 defines the Lutheran churches.
summary: The churches that follow Luther's teaching, the state churches of Scandinavia.

name: Reformed (Calvinist)
date_note: Zwingli begins preaching reform at Zürich in 1519; Calvin's Geneva follows from 1536.
summary: The churches of Zwingli and Calvin, including the Presbyterian and Dutch Reformed churches.

name: Anabaptism
date_note: The first adult baptisms in Zürich, January 1525.
summary: Believers' baptism and non-violence: the Mennonites, Amish and Hutterites.

name: Anglicanism
date_note: The Act of Supremacy, 1534.
summary: The Church of England and the worldwide Anglican Communion.

name: Baptists
date_note: John Smyth's English exile congregation in Amsterdam, 1609.
summary: Congregations that baptise believers by immersion; the largest Protestant family in the United States.

name: Quakers
date_note: George Fox's vision on Pendle Hill, 1652.
summary: The Religious Society of Friends: silent worship, no clergy, and a long witness for peace.

name: Methodism
date_note: John Wesley's Aldersgate experience, London, 1738.
summary: A revival inside the Church of England that became its own church, stressing personal holiness.

name: Seventh-day Adventism
date_note: The church was organised in 1863, after the Millerite movement of the 1840s.
summary: A church that keeps Saturday as the Sabbath and expects Christ's imminent return.

name: Latter Day Saints
date_note: Joseph Smith organised the church in Fayette, New York, in 1830.
summary: A restorationist church with the Book of Mormon as added scripture, centred in Utah.

name: Jehovah's Witnesses
date_note: Charles Taze Russell began Zion's Watch Tower in Pittsburgh in 1879.
summary: A millenarian movement that rejects the Trinity and evangelises door to door.

name: Pentecostalism
date_note: The Azusa Street Revival, Los Angeles, 1906 (preceded by Topeka, 1901). It grew from the Methodist Holiness movement.
summary: Spirit-filled worship with speaking in tongues and healing, the fastest-growing Christian movement of the 20th century.

name: Rastafari
date_note: Arises in Jamaica after Haile Selassie's coronation in 1930.
summary: A Jamaican movement that honours Haile Selassie and looks to Africa, Ethiopia above all, as Zion.

name: Islam
date_note: Tradition dates the first revelation to Muhammad to 610.
summary: Submission to the one God as revealed in the Qur'an to the Prophet Muhammad. The second largest religion in the world.

name: Sunni Islam
date_note: The community divides over the succession to Muhammad from his death in 632; 'Sunni' as a name and school forms over the next centuries.
summary: The majority of Muslims, who accepted the first caliphs and follow the four schools of law.

name: Shia Islam
date_note: The party of Ali forms from 632; the killing of Husayn at Karbala in 680 makes it a distinct tradition.
summary: Muslims who hold that leadership passed to Ali and the Imams of his line; the majority in Iran and Iraq.

name: Ibadi Islam
date_note: Grows among moderate Kharijites in Basra in the late 7th c.
summary: The third branch of Islam, neither Sunni nor Shia, still the majority school in Oman.

name: Sufism
date_note: Ascetic movements of the 8th c. in Iraq; the orders (tariqas) form from the 12th c.
summary: The inward, mystical path of Islam, taught through masters and orders across both Sunni and Shia worlds.

name: Ismailism
date_note: Splits from the Shia majority over the succession to Ja'far al-Sadiq, who died in 765.
summary: A Shia branch with a living Imam, today the Aga Khan.

name: Druze
date_note: Proclaimed in Fatimid Cairo in 1017; closed to converts since 1043.
summary: An esoteric faith that grew from Ismailism and has accepted no converts since 1043, living in Lebanon, Syria and Israel.

name: Ahmadiyya
date_note: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad took the oath of allegiance from followers in 1889.
summary: A movement founded in British India that most other Muslims do not recognise as Islamic.

name: Bábism
date_note: The Báb declared his mission in Shiraz in 1844; after 1866 most Bábís followed Bahá'u'lláh. A small Azali remnant lasted longer.
ended_by: Most followers became Bahá'ís in the 1860s.
summary: A messianic movement in Qajar Iran whose prophet, the Báb, was executed in 1850.

name: Bahá'í Faith
date_note: Bahá'u'lláh's declaration in the Ridván garden, Baghdad, 1863.
summary: A faith teaching the unity of God, of religion and of humanity, with its world centre at Haifa.

name: Mandaeism
date_note: Origins between the 1st and 3rd c. CE are debated; Mandaean texts point to the Jordan valley, the attested community to southern Mesopotamia.
summary: A small gnostic baptismal religion that honours John the Baptist, long rooted in the marshes of southern Iraq and Iran.

name: Historical Vedic religion
date_note: The Rigveda is usually dated c. 1500–1200 BCE. Its sacrificial religion turns into classical Hinduism from about 500 BCE; it did not die so much as become something else.
ended_by: Grew into classical Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism reacted against it.
summary: The fire-sacrifice religion of the Vedas, the oldest layer beneath Hinduism.

name: Hinduism
date_note: Classical Hinduism takes shape from about 500 BCE as Vedic ritual meets the epics, the Upanishads and local devotion. Many Hindus see their dharma as without beginning.
summary: A family of traditions sharing the Vedas, dharma, karma and rebirth, and devotion to many forms of the divine. The third largest religion.

name: Vaishnavism
date_note: The Heliodorus pillar at Vidisha (c. 113 BCE) is early hard evidence of devotion to Vishnu-Vasudeva.
summary: Devotion to Vishnu and his avatars, Krishna and Rama above all.

name: Shaivism
date_note: Shiva worship is older; organised Shaiva movements such as the Pashupatas are attested from the first centuries CE.
summary: Devotion to Shiva as the supreme god, from temple ritual to Kashmir's philosophy.

name: Shaktism
date_note: The Devi Mahatmya, c. 5th–6th c. CE, is the founding text of goddess-centred worship.
summary: Worship of the Goddess, Devi or Shakti, as the supreme power.

name: Smartism
date_note: Associated with Adi Shankara (8th c.).
summary: A tradition that honours five deities equally, linked to Shankara's non-dualist philosophy.

name: Lingayatism
date_note: Grows around Basava at Kalyana in the 12th c.
summary: A Shaiva movement that rejected caste and temple ritual; its members wear a personal linga.

name: Gaudiya Vaishnavism
date_note: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's movement in Bengal, early 16th c.
summary: Ecstatic devotion to Krishna, carried worldwide by ISKCON (the 'Hare Krishnas') since 1966.

name: Jainism
date_note: Mahavira is placed in the 6th–5th c. BCE; Jains hold him to be the last of 24 teachers, the 23rd of whom, Parshvanatha, is earlier.
summary: A path of non-violence toward every living being and self-discipline toward the soul's release.

name: Buddhism
date_note: The Buddha's dates are debated; many scholars now place his death around 400 BCE, older tradition in the 6th c. BCE.
summary: The teaching of the Buddha: suffering, its cause, its end and the path to it.

name: Theravada
date_note: Its lineage reaches Sri Lanka with Mahinda in the 3rd c. BCE; the name Theravada is applied later.
summary: The 'way of the elders', with the Pali canon; the Buddhism of Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.

name: Mahayana
date_note: Mahayana sutras appear from around the 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE.
summary: The 'great vehicle' of the bodhisattva ideal; the Buddhism of China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

name: Pure Land Buddhism
date_note: Huiyuan's society on Mount Lu, 402; Hōnen founds the Japanese Jōdo school in 1175.
summary: Devotion to Amitabha Buddha and rebirth in his Pure Land, the most widespread Buddhism in East Asia.

name: Chan / Zen
date_note: Traditionally from Bodhidharma, c. 500; historically the Chan school forms in the 7th–8th c.
summary: Meditation-centred Buddhism: Chan in China, Seon in Korea, Thiền in Vietnam, Zen in Japan.

name: Vajrayana
date_note: Buddhist tantras appear in India from the 7th c.
summary: Tantric Buddhism, the Buddhism of Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia.

name: Nichiren Buddhism
date_note: Nichiren first chanted the title of the Lotus Sutra in 1253.
summary: Japanese Buddhism centred on the Lotus Sutra and the chant Nam-myoho-renge-kyo.

name: Navayana
date_note: B. R. Ambedkar and about half a million followers converted at Nagpur on 14 October 1956.
summary: Ambedkar's 'new vehicle', a Buddhism of social liberation for India's Dalits.

name: Ājīvika
date_note: Founded by Makkhali Gosala, a contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira. Last mentioned in Tamil inscriptions of the 14th c.
ended_by: Faded away in medieval South India; no texts of its own survive.
summary: An ascetic school that held that everything is fixed by destiny (niyati).

name: Sikhism
date_note: Guru Nanak's revelation at Sultanpur Lodhi is dated to about 1499 (the old file used 1469, his birth year).
summary: The faith of the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib: one God, honest work and service.

name: Khalsa
date_note: Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa at Anandpur on Vaisakhi, 1699.
summary: The order of initiated Sikhs, who keep the five Ks.

name: Chinese folk religion
date_note: Shang oracle bones from c. 1250 BCE are the earliest written record of the ancestor and spirit cults that run through Chinese religion.
summary: The worship of ancestors, local gods and spirits that underlies Chinese life, mixing freely with Daoism and Buddhism.

name: Confucianism
date_note: Confucius lived 551–479 BCE.
summary: The ethics of ritual, family and good government taught by Confucius, the state ideology of imperial China, Korea and Vietnam.

name: Daoism
date_note: The Laozi and Zhuangzi texts date to about the 4th c. BCE.
summary: The way of the Dao: harmony with the natural course of things, from philosophy to temple religion.

name: Way of the Celestial Masters
date_note: Zhang Daoling's revelation from Laozi in 142 CE.
summary: The first organised Daoist church, still alive as the Zhengyi school.

name: Quanzhen Daoism
date_note: Wang Chongyang's school, founded around 1170.
summary: Monastic Daoism of inner alchemy, the main Daoist order in China today.

name: Shinto
date_note: Kami worship is prehistoric; Shinto as a codified tradition dates from the Kojiki (712) and the shrine system of the Nara court. The old file's 500 BCE had no source.
summary: The way of the kami, worshipped at shrines across Japan.

name: State Shinto
date_note: Created by the Meiji government in 1868; abolished by the Shinto Directive of December 1945.
ended_by: Abolished by the Allied Shinto Directive, 15 December 1945.
summary: Shinto turned into a national ideology around the emperor, imposed across the Japanese empire.

name: Tenrikyo
date_note: Nakayama Miki's revelation, 1838.
summary: One of Japan's first new religions, teaching the 'joyous life' under God the Parent.

name: Cheondoism
date_note: Choe Je-u founded Donghak ('Eastern Learning') in 1860; it took the name Cheondogyo in 1905.
summary: A Korean religion teaching that every human being bears heaven within.

name: Caodaism
date_note: Formally founded in 1926.
summary: A Vietnamese religion that unites Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism, Christianity and spiritism under one God.

name: Zoroastrianism
date_note: Zarathustra's date is unknown; estimates run from about 1500 to 500 BCE. 1000 BCE is a midpoint, not a fact.
summary: The faith of Zarathustra: the wise lord Ahura Mazda against the lie, good thoughts, good words, good deeds.

name: Manichaeism
date_note: Mani began preaching in 240. Last traces are in Fujian, China, around the 16th–17th c.
ended_by: Persecuted in both the Roman and Chinese empires; it outlived its rivals in China and vanished there last.
summary: Mani's religion of light against darkness. For a millennium it reached from Carthage to China.

name: Yazidism
date_note: Formed around Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir (died 1162) on older Iranian foundations.
summary: A Kurdish faith of one God and seven holy beings led by the Peacock Angel.

name: Sumerian religion
date_note: Temples at Uruk from the 4th millennium BCE. Sumerian ends as a spoken language around 2000 BCE; its gods live on in Babylonian religion.
ended_by: Absorbed into Akkadian and Babylonian religion.
summary: The oldest recorded religion, of city gods such as Inanna and Enlil housed in ziggurats.

name: Babylonian & Assyrian religion
date_note: The last datable cuneiform temple tablet is from about 75 CE. Some cults survived later at Harran.
ended_by: Faded under Persian, Hellenistic and Parthian rule.
summary: The cults of Marduk, Ashur and Ishtar, and the astronomy that served them.

name: Ancient Egyptian religion
date_note: From the unification of Egypt, c. 3100 BCE, to the closing of the Isis temple at Philae, dated c. 535–537 CE.
ended_by: Christianisation; Justinian closed the last temple, at Philae.
summary: The gods of the Nile, the pharaoh's divine kingship and the judgement of the dead.

name: Canaanite & Phoenician religion
date_note: Bronze Age Canaan to the end of Punic worship in Roman North Africa, c. 4th c. CE.
summary: The religion of El, Baal and Asherah, carried west by Phoenician sailors to Carthage and Spain.

name: Ancient Greek religion
date_note: Several Olympian gods are named in Mycenaean Linear B tablets (c. 1400 BCE). Public sacrifice was banned in 391–392 CE; the Athens Academy closed in 529.
ended_by: Christian emperors banned the cults (391–392); philosophy schools closed in 529.
summary: Zeus and the Olympians, the mysteries of Eleusis and the oracle of Delphi.

name: Ancient Roman religion
date_note: From Rome's traditional founding (753 BCE) to the Theodosian ban on pagan sacrifice (391–392). The old file's 380 Edict of Thessalonica made Christianity official but did not ban the old cults.
summary: The state cult of Jupiter, the household gods and the deified emperors.

name: Mithraism
date_note: First attested in the late 1st c. CE; gone by about 400. (The old file stored this as '1st century', which broke its JSON.)
ended_by: Banned with the other pagan cults by 392.
summary: A Roman mystery cult of the god Mithras, popular with soldiers, worshipped in underground temples.

name: Germanic & Norse religion
date_note: Iron Age roots; Norse forms are best known from the Viking Age. Sweden is the last kingdom to become Christian, around 1100.
ended_by: Christianisation of the Germanic peoples and of Scandinavia.
summary: The gods Odin, Thor and Freyja, the world-tree and the sagas.

name: Heathenry (Ásatrú)
date_note: Iceland recognised the Ásatrúarfélagið in 1973; it was founded in 1972.
summary: A modern revival of Germanic religion.

name: Celtic religion
date_note: Hallstatt and La Tène cultures from about 600 BCE; Ireland is largely Christian by about 600 CE.
summary: Druids, sacred groves and gods such as Lugus, known mostly from Roman writers and archaeology.

name: Slavic religion
date_note: From the Slavic migrations (6th c.) to the destruction of the temple at Arkona in 1168.
ended_by: Christianisation; Arkona fell to the Danes in 1168.
summary: Perun, Veles and the household spirits of the Slavs.

name: Baltic religion
date_note: Lithuania, the last pagan state in Europe, was baptised in 1387.
ended_by: Crusades and the baptism of Lithuania in 1387.
summary: Perkūnas the thunder god and the sacred fire of the Baltic peoples.

name: Wicca
date_note: Made public by Gerald Gardner's Witchcraft Today, 1954.
summary: A modern pagan witchcraft honouring a goddess and a god through the turning year.

name: Maya religion
date_note: Ceremonial centres from about 1000 BCE. Nojpetén, the last independent Maya kingdom, fell in 1697; Maya ritual continues today blended with Catholicism.
ended_by: Spanish conquest; the last kingdom fell in 1697.
summary: The calendar priests, kings and gods of the Maya, recorded in glyphs and the Popol Vuh.

name: Mexica (Aztec) religion
date_note: From the founding of Tenochtitlan (1325) to its fall (1521). It drew on older Mesoamerican religion.
summary: Huitzilopochtli, Tlaloc and the Templo Mayor at the heart of the Aztec empire.

name: Inca religion
date_note: From the rise of Cusco (c. 1200) to the fall of Vilcabamba (1572). It drew on older Andean religion.
summary: Inti the sun, the huacas and the Sapa Inca as child of the sun.

name: Native American Church
date_note: Incorporated in Oklahoma in 1918.
summary: A peyote-centred faith practised by many Native American nations.

name: Yoruba religion (Ifá, Orisha)
date_note: Ile-Ife flourishes from about 1000 CE; the religion's roots are older and undated.
summary: Olodumare, the orishas and the Ifá divination system of the Yoruba.

name: Vodun
date_note: Recorded in the kingdom of Dahomey from the 17th c.; roots older.
summary: The vodun spirits of the Fon and Ewe peoples of Benin and Togo.

name: Haitian Vodou
date_note: Forms among enslaved Africans in Saint-Domingue in the 18th c.
summary: Fon, Kongo and Yoruba spirits served alongside Catholic saints in Haiti.

name: Santería (Lucumí)
date_note: Organised in 19th-c. Cuba.
summary: Yoruba orisha worship in Cuba, paired with Catholic saints.

name: Candomblé
date_note: The Casa Branca terreiro in Salvador dates from around 1830.
summary: An Afro-Brazilian religion of the orixás (the orisha spirits), kept alive in the terreiros (temple communities) of Bahia.
